narrative:
The model predicts you have a 42% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The prediction is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. By far the strongest factor is that you have already failed two classes in the past. Among students who passed, the average number of previous failures is zero, so this history strongly pushes the model toward expecting you will fail again.

The second most important factor is that your guardian is someone other than your mother or father. This is quite unusual—most students who pass have a parent as guardian—and it pulls the prediction slightly toward passing, acting as a small positive influence.

Third, your weekend alcohol consumption is very low. This is actually better than most students who pass and therefore works in your favor, nudging the prediction a little toward passing.

Even though two of these factors lean slightly positive, your past failures outweigh them and drive the overall prediction that you are at serious risk. To improve, you should focus immediately on creating a structured study plan, seeking extra academic support, and making sure you understand the material from those two classes you failed before. Addressing those gaps now is the clearest way to raise your chances of passing.
